question: Which statement about the lower bound for sorting is correct?
options: Any comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons on average; non-comparison sorts such as counting sort can achieve O(n) when keys are integers in a small range.
Merge sort sorts in O(n) average time; the Ω(n log n) bound applies only to the worst case, not the average case.
Every sorting algorithm obeys the ⌈log₂(n!)⌉ comparison lower bound, including counting sort; for 13 elements the exact minimum is 33 comparisons.
Radix sort beats the Ω(n log n) bound asymptotically for all inputs because it uses comparisons more efficiently.
gold_answer: Any comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons on average; non-comparison sorts such as counting sort can achieve O(n) when keys are integers in a small range.
notes: All quoted passages were read live on 2026-11-19 from the three CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikipedia articles cited in the evidence. The comparison-sort lower bound and the sorting-numbers result for 13 elements are checked against the cited pages; re-verify the exact sentences before freezing.

positions.answer: Any comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons on average; non-comparison sorts such as counting sort can achieve O(n) when keys are integers in a small range.

claims.text: A comparison sort must have an average-case lower bound of Ω(n log n) comparison operations.

evidence.text: There are fundamental limits on the performance of comparison sorts. A comparison sort must have an average-case lower bound of Ω(n log n) comparison operations, which is known as linearithmic time.
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Performance limits and advantages of different sorting techniques section.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states the average-case Ω(n log n) comparison lower bound almost word for word.

claims.text: Non-comparison sorts can achieve O(n) performance by using operations other than comparisons, sidestepping the comparison-sort lower bound.

evidence.text: Non-comparison sorts (such as the examples discussed below) can achieve O(n) performance by using operations other than comparisons, allowing them to sidestep this lower bound (assuming elements are constant-sized).
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Performance limits and advantages of different sorting techniques section.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states that non-comparison sorts reach O(n) by using other operations and thereby sidestep the lower bound, which entails the claim.

claims.text: Counting sort runs in linear time when the keys form a range that is small compared to n.

evidence.text: When the keys form a small (compared to n) range, counting sort is an example algorithm that runs in linear time.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage gives the same small-range condition and the same linear-time result for counting sort.

positions.answer: Merge sort sorts in O(n) average time; the Ω(n log n) bound applies only to the worst case, not the average case.

claims.text: Merge sort has an average-case running time of O(n) comparisons.

evidence.text: In sorting n objects, merge sort has an average and worst-case performance of O(n log n) comparisons.
In this sense, mergesort, heapsort, and introsort are asymptotically optimal in terms of the number of comparisons they must perform, although this metric neglects other operations.
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Performance limits and advantages of different sorting techniques section.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passages give merge sort O(n log n) average comparisons and call it asymptotically optimal, both of which refute a linear average-case bound.

claims.text: The Ω(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorting applies only to the worst case, not the average case.

evidence.text: A comparison sort must have an average-case lower bound of Ω(n log n) comparison operations, which is known as linearithmic time.
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Performance limits and advantages of different sorting techniques section.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage explicitly calls the Ω(n log n) bound an average-case lower bound, directly denying that it is worst-case only.

claims.text: Merge sort requires O(n) auxiliary space.

evidence.text: In this sense, mergesort, heapsort, and introsort are asymptotically optimal in terms of the number of comparisons they must perform, although this metric neglects other operations.
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Performance limits and advantages of different sorting techniques section.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage discusses only comparison counts and says nothing about memory usage, so it is topical to merge sort but neither establishes nor refutes a space bound.

positions.answer: Every sorting algorithm obeys the ⌈log₂(n!)⌉ comparison lower bound, including counting sort; for 13 elements the exact minimum is 33 comparisons.

claims.text: Counting sort is subject to the same ⌈log₂(n!)⌉ comparison lower bound as comparison sorts.

evidence.text: Some sorting problems admit a strictly faster solution than the Ω(n log n) bound for comparison sorting by using non-comparison sorts; an example is integer sorting, where all keys are integers. When the keys form a small (compared to n) range, counting sort is an example algorithm that runs in linear time.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage identifies counting sort as a non-comparison sort that breaks the comparison-sort bound by running in linear time, so it refutes applying the comparison lower bound to counting sort.

claims.text: The minimal number of comparisons needed to sort 13 elements is 33.

evidence.text: For example, ⌈log₂(13!)⌉ = 33, but the minimal number of comparisons to sort 13 elements has been proved to be 34.
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Number of comparisons required to sort a list section.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states the proven minimum is 34 while 33 is only the ⌈log₂(n!)⌉ lower bound, directly refuting the claimed minimum.

claims.text: At least log₂(n!) comparisons are needed on average to sort n items, because a comparison gives at most one bit of information.

evidence.text: Since a comparison can give only two results, the maximum amount of information it provides is 1 bit. Therefore, after k comparisons the remaining entropy of the permutation, given the results of those comparisons, is at least log₂(n!) − k bits on average. To perform the sort, complete information is needed, so the remaining entropy must be 0. It follows that k must be at least log₂(n!) on average.
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Lower bound for the average number of comparisons section.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage derives the one-bit-per-comparison premise and the log₂(n!) average-case bound, which together entail the claim.
